review:
Turok 2 was initially released on the Nintendo 64 in 1998, and it could've been a contender. It had enemy scripting and graphics comparable to Half-Life, sprawling levels flush with secrets, a rogue's gallery of half-a-dozen beautifully rendered non-human cultures to slaughter, a far superior arsenal to any first person shooter on the market, a grander scope than most western console roleplaying games of the era, split-screen multiplayer with multiple game modes, a robust cheat engine and options suite, a voluptuous and scantily clad blue woman with a thigh gap, and a shirtless Native American hero tasked with murdering everything in the interdimensional sewer he's sworn to preserve. 

It was the greatest first person shooter of its generation by a significant margin, and you know I'm qualified to make that statement because I've lived almost my entire life in first person. It was better than Half-Life, Goldeneye, Blood, Shadow Warrior, Unreal, System Shock 2, Medal of Honor, Chex Quest, or Realms of the Haunting.

It was also impossible to play. The mad taint of Turok 2's dizzying graphical ambitions consigned it to oblivion until Night Dive remade it in 2017 once computing was advanced enough to accommodate the grandeur therein. Before that? Good luck hitting anything. On the N64, Turok 2 had a draw distance shorter than many rooms were large, and it ran at twenty frames per second when nothing was happening on the screen.

There was never nothing happening onscreen. Between the bloom lighting, the high res world assets, the huge scope of everything, the detailed and often animated weapon models, the real time shadows, the complex wiggle worm rigging and high polygon count on every enemy, and the preposterous floods-of-blood death animations resulting from explosions, Turok 2's framerate dipped into the single digits somewhere approaching most of the time. If you had more than one enemy on the screen, the framerate was now your enemy, as well. This was especially true if you used the N64 RAM expansion because it let you set the resolution to a whopping 480i, and of course you did that because you were 8 years old, you wanted the game to look as good as possible, and you probably didn't make the connection between the resolution and the framerate. The RAM expansion, despite living up to its namesake, only compounded the problem, swelling up a game that was already way too big for its breeches. 

Now, combine that with the terrible N64 analog stick, lack of dual analog control, look spring by default, and highly mobile enemies that demanded precision aiming, and you've got yourself an exercise in whatever emotion you feel when video game don't work good.

Turok 2 was full of so much stellar material that it didn't work. It was ahead of its time, ahead of its hardware, ahead of its interface, ahead of its scene, ahead of itself, and to play it was forbidden by its very existence. It brought the N64 to its knees, I imagine it brought most 1999 computers to their knees when it got ported to PC, and it took being remade nearly twenty years later for its brilliance to finally be realized. Turok 2 wasn't bad for being unplayable on the N64, no. The N64 was bad for not being able to play Turok 2.

Turok 2: Seeds of Evil is the sequel to the previous game in the series, Turok: Dinosaur Hunter. Much like it's predecessor, it is an FPS game were you will take on the role of a man named Turok (But not the same guy from the previous game.) to kill dinosaurs, monsters, aliens while you explore large, sprawling levels. And just like the previous game, it originally came out on the N64, with an initial PC port that was just as bad as the PC port of the first game. But again, Nightdive Studios released a proper port. I played the N64 version way back in the day, but never managed to finish it, even when using cheat codes. I am also biased towards Turok 2 slightly more than the first game, purely because it was the game I played first, but both games have their own charm and solid gameplay.

Compared to the first game, Turok 2 has a bit more focus on story this time around, having proper cutscenes, something that the third game would go even further with later on. The plot involves an alien that got awakened after the ending of the first game, and stopping his plans to destroy the universe. Simple and easy. It offers more narrative than the first game, but less than the third, which I think is the perfect sweet spot.

Unlike the first game though, you wont just navigate levels to find keys and reach the end like the first one. Every level involves various mission objectives, like rescuing captured children or destroying ammo caches. You MUST complete these objectives before reaching the end of the stage or else you won't be able complete the level. Keys still need to be found to access later levels. Graphics, animations and shooting mechanics have been improved. Saving works differently this time around too. Rather than having specific spots where you can save the game, Turok 2 allows you to save anywhere at anytime, which some people would say makes the game too easy, but trust me when I say this: Playing through Hardcore difficulty in the Hive of Mantids, when you get to that room with those turrets on the ceiling? You'll thank God that quicksaving and quickloading is a thing.

Positives include:

- Boss battles: There are only four bosses in the game, but I think they are an improvement over the bosses from Turok: Dinosaur Hunter. Small enemies might show up, you have to stand in a certain spot to avoid damage, and shoot specific parts of the boss to damage them. They aren't perfect and some might consider the fights to be gimmicky, but they are more engaging than the "walk-backwards-and-shot-until-the-enemy-dies" from the the first game.

- Weapons: Turok 2 has more weapons this time around and they are greater in variety, including a flamethrower, charge dart rifle to eletrocute enemies and the infamous cerebral bore, a weapon that most people think of when they think of Turok 2 (It even inspire the name of a Scottish death-metal band). The shooting in general feels better, as you have a proper crosshair this time around.

- Music: The tracks you hear throughut the game are very good, fitting the mood of each level you visit. The theme for the Port of Adia is burnt into my brain, along with theme of the final level.

- Enemies: There is great enemy variety here. bio-engineered dinosaurs, bugs with energy weapons, giant brutes etc. They all have unique sounds, animations and some of them act smarter than enemies from the first game that would just rush towards you or shot at you while standing still in one spot. Some enmies will take cover, run away or even blow themselves up before they die to try and damage you. The animations and gore for the enemies is also vastly improved, shooting them in certain spots with certain weapons will make body parts be blown off or apart. Blowing a giant hole through the chest of enemies is also something you'll see. There are no humans this time around, just you and a bunch of other disgusting freaks to shoot.

Negatives include:

- Level design: The first game had 8 levels in total, while Turok 2 only has 6, albeit much larger and complex than those in the first game.  Turok 2's levels has been a point of contention back when the game first came out and is still are to this day. They are massive and maze-like, with backtracking and thorough exploration a necessity to get to the end AND complete all objectives. I really like that the levels are large, but compared to the first game, a lot of the time you are walking in identical-looking hallways with not enough landmarks. Having played and replayed the game as much as I did, this is not an issue for me, but for anyone else playing the game for the first time, simply getting to the end of the level could be a very frustrating experience, even more so when you find out that you missed saving one kid or sealing a tunnel and have to go back. One of the QoL features included in the game is having objective markers, but these only appear when you are close to something and it can be turned of if you want the original experience.

"Lair Of The Blind Ones" will probably awaken some awful memories for people who played through the game during the N64 days, when internet guides weren't as numerous and accessible as now. All the issues I mentioned earlier about going through identical corridors become the absolute worst in this level. I personally don't think it is as bad as many people claim it is, but it is my least liked level in the game, and my suggestion is that you check up on a guide for the first time you play through it, just to save yourself the frustration of getting lost or missing an objective.

- Multiplayer: This version of Turok 2 has the option for online multiplayer PvP with dedicated servers, but these were only active early on when the game came out on steam. The multiplayer scene is mostly dead, last I checked. Unless you can get some friends to play with you, you're probably not going to experience it. From what I heard from other people, the multplayer felt janky, so you're not missing out on much.

- Less dinosaurs: If you don't count the weird, humanoid dinosaur hybrids, you barely get to fight or meet dinosaurs. You come across generic "raptor" enemies that you will encounter, and at one point you get to ride on the back of a Styracosaurus. There is a distinct lack of dinosaurs compared to the first game. This is a cardinal sin, in my opinion.

Final thoughts:
All in all, Turok 2 is a worthy sequel to the first game, but not perfect. Still, I consider the series to have peaked here, as I find the third game to be worse than the first two, and every game afterwards ranged from mediocre to bad. If you like the first game, then I can recommmend Turok 2. Just be prepared for large levels that can be overwhelming for a first time player.

A legendary game!

If you're looking for ultra-realistic graphics, forget it. Now… if you want pure fun, no nonsense, then Turok 2: Seeds of Evil is a must-play. This game is the definition of true retro: creative weapons (the legendary Cerebral Bore), levels full of exploration, an immersive soundtrack, and that kind of challenge that makes every bit of progress feel rewarding. This is not a game that holds your hand. It throws you into the world and says: “figure it out.” And that’s exactly what makes it so good. The Steam version brings modern improvements without losing its essence, it’s still that brutal, weird, and incredibly fun 90s classic.

If you value gameplay above everything else, this is an easy recommendation. Turok 2 hasn’t aged, it has only become more legendary.

[h1]Rating[/h1]
4/10

[h1]Intro[/h1]
Admittedly, throughout my years of owning this, I repeatedly start a new campaign and stop before I even finish the first level. I also don't remember what it was like to play the first game, which I did score high a few years back. But every time I return to this, I'm reminded of why I keep giving up. From the first level, there's so many dead ends and poor signposting, that I end up having no hope for the levels that proceed it. It may have great combat with positive feedback and creative enemies, but it's all unfortunately inside this mess of a maze.

[h1]Positives[/h1]
+ Good soundtrack.
+ Great enemy variety.
+ Great weapon variety.
+ Weapons have great impact.
+ Good aesthetics and graphics.

[h1]Negatives[/h1]
- Enemies frequently respawn. Further confusing me whenever I got lost.
- Poor level design. It often has me hitting dead ends after picking up a key or pressing a button. In fact, it would really benefit from the GPS that they introduced in the remaster for Quake 2, but it's yet to be retroactively patched in here.

І навіть попри це, я люблю другу части Турка, вважаю її гідним продовженням, яке варто пройти, хоча би раз, щоб отримати трохи більше сюжету та приємного досвіду від, того що тобі звичайний моб знімає одною атакою чверть хепе:). Tremendo juego. Fue como revivir parte de mi infancia de cuando tenia una Nintendo 64 hace como 20 años y regresar de la escuela y ponerme a jugar Turok 2: Seeds of Evil todas las tardes. No me queda más que recomendar este juego.
é sempre uma delícia jogar Turok, tinha jogado ele em 99 no nintendo 64 e já era super fã da franquia. estou jogando e esperando ancioso pelo turok origins.

Turok 2: Seeds of Evil se ríe en la cara del cliché de “la secuela es peor”. Si el primer Turok era brutalidad pura 90’s sin filtro, esta entrega es la respuesta a la pregunta ¿Cómo podemos hacer el juego mejor? Y alguien con los huevos suficientes respondió "Si".

El salto a Nintendo 64 no fue solo una mejora técnica, fue el punto fuerte. Los polígonos de 64-bit, restaurados en HD sin intentar ocultar su origen, tienen el encanto exacto de esa era final de los 90: afilados, angulosos y gloriosos. No intentan modernizarse, intentan recordarte. Y eso lo vuelve hermoso.

Más difícil. Más injusto. Más necesario pensar. Los enemigos no vienen a pelear: vienen a destrozarte. Son duros, rápidos, coordinados, y cualquier error hace que te comas la pantalla del Game Over. Los precipicios siguen siendo tu rival oculto, ahora acompañados por pantanos tóxicos y charcos venenosos que te instakillean. Sí, las vidas siguen estando. Sí, respawn desde el último guardado. Porque los 90 nunca se fueron. Pero ojo a la mejora real: ahora podes guardar cuando te dé la gana. Una mejora que era obligatoria y el que este es un verdadero alivio.

La historia, ¿La entiendo? No. ¿Hay un villano malo maloso que quiere arrasar el universo y yo debo impedirlo con exceso de violencia? Sí. Pero ahora tenés a Adon, una waifu que te asigna objetivos en cada mundo. La potencia de la época le permitió al juego introducir elementos narrativos, con voces para un par de personajes, Adon y el chaman que nos da los poderes a cambio de las plumas, son el claro ejemplo, así como cinámicas. Un excelente detalle que no pasa desapercibido.

Nuevas armas. Nuevas interacciones. Nueva arma secreta por ensamblar. Más salvajismo creativo. Ahora además hay un sistema de “poderes” que, aunque interesante conceptualmente, solo puede activarse en puntos específicos del mapa. Idea genial… ejecución un poco desaprovechada. Se perdona porque todo lo demás vuela la tapa de los sesos. A lo largo de la partida te vas dando cuenta de los puntos críticos, los headhsot pueden hacer instakill si esta bien dados por ejemplo, aunque el aumentar la vida máxima con el cuchillo y los demás secretitos del Turok desaparecieron, fueron reemplazados por mas vida en el gameplay, un trato justo si me lo preguntaran.

Un poco personal al respecto pero, el lobby inicial donde están todos los portales y la cámara central me recodaba a el Crash Bandicoot 3: Warped, cada vez que terminaba el mundo y volvía, una neura en mi proyectaba esa imagen. No se si fui el único pero teniendo en cuenta que ambos juegos se suponen que salieron en el mismo año, me parece un detalle curioso.

Y ahora el punto mas fuerte del juego, los enemigos, una absoluta bestialidad si tenemos en cuenta la época. Es increíble que en 1998 se haya podido crear una inteligencia artificial tan avanzada: Los enemigos pueden pelear entre sí. Reaccionan al lugar de los disparos: si los atacas de forma no letal, buscan cobertura para esconderse. Si los quemas con el lanzallamas, corren como pollos sin cabeza, y si hay agua una fuente de agua cerca, como un río o charco se tiraran para apagar las llamas. Cada mundo introduce enemigos diferentes y únicos, evitando la monotonía y ayudando a que la experiencia nunca se vuelva repetitiva. Los jefes también destacan, con peleas desafiantes que te obligan a aprender su patrón de ataque. Aunque sí, algunas peleas en dificultad extrema pueden volverse un poco tediosas, pero no se descarta el método clásico de vaciarles el cargador de plomo como en la primera entrega.

Turok 2 Seeds of Evil puede ser un poco tedioso de completar al 100% y es obligatorio el uso de una guía en muchos puntos, es absolutamente mejor en todo lo de la primera entrega y, al jugar los dos juegos seguidos, se puede ver aún mas como el estudio de desarrollo se puso la meta de hacer un mejor juego, rompiendo la premisa del principio, no todas las secuelas son malas. Totalmente recomendado.

It's Turok 2. Excellent game and kind of ahead of the curb for the time on consoles. 
I remember when I was a teenager playing this game, it seemed so hard, but with modern controls, it's really pretty easy, save for the occasional level design confusion, but Nightdive has done an excellent job at updating it with better navigation and some of the maps have been reworked, but I honestly like it like that. I remember the lair of the blind ones being a slog, but with the remaster, it wasn't too bad. 
Anyway, if you are nostalgic over this diamond in the rough or if you've never played it and want a decent retro shooter that's pretty forgiving (there is a hardcore difficulty, if you prefer) with cool weapons (mostly) and a unique setting, I highly recommend it. 
It's a solid good time, but you may wanna have a guide handy for finding all the keys and macguffins.
